subject: Critical Thinking
title: A Brief History of Fallacy Hunting
description: A quick win: understand A Brief History of Fallacy Hunting.

hook.text: Aristotle was the first fallacy hunter. His 'Sophistical Refutations' in 350 BC was the original myth-busting guide.

buildup.text: He identified tricks used by Sophists — paid teachers of persuasion who cared about winning, not truth.

discovery.text: Medieval scholars expanded the list. John Stuart Mill, Bentham, and Schopenhauer added new categories in the 1800s.

twist.text: Today we have over 100 named fallacies. Yet political ads, social media, and daily arguments use the same ancient ones.

climax.text: The tools to detect flawed reasoning have existed for 2,400 years. We just don't teach them in school.

punchline.text: Aristotle gave us the playbook. We forgot to read it.

quiz.question: Who first systematically cataloged logical fallacies?

details.summary: Aristotle first catalogued fallacies in his Sophistical Refutations over 2,300 years ago. Since then, philosophers have expanded the list from 13 original fallacies to hundreds, reflecting humanity's enduring struggle with flawed reasoning.
details.whyItMatters: The long history of fallacy hunting shows that flawed reasoning is a permanent feature of human cognition, not a modern problem with a quick fix.
takeaways: Aristotle identified the first 13 fallacies around 350 BCE
The list has grown to hundreds of recognized fallacies
Each new communication medium creates new fallacy patterns

faq.question: What were Aristotle's original categories of fallacies?
faq.answer: Aristotle divided fallacies into those dependent on language (ambiguity, equivocation) and those independent of language (accident, irrelevant conclusion). This basic division between linguistic and logical errors persists in modern classifications.

faq.question: Have new types of fallacies emerged in the digital age?
faq.answer: Yes. The Gish Gallop thrives on social media, algorithmic cherry-picking creates filter-bubble fallacies, and deepfakes create new forms of false evidence. The medium changes how fallacies operate and spread.
